evidence: submit(actor, payload: HoursPayload) passes its input to this.payroll.submitHours(employeeId, payload.week, payload.hours) and then calls this.audit.log(actor, 'submit', sheet.id). Both are business-layer services, which presentation may call.
approve(actor, timesheetId) calls this.payroll.approve(timesheetId) and returns { approved: sheet.approved }. The approval decision is made in the business layer.
export(week) returns (await this.payroll.run(week)).map(payslipRow).join('\n'). This formats output using the presentation view payslipRow.
The constructor injects PayrollService and PayrollAuditService from src/business/services, which is dependency wiring from a layer presentation may depend on.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: PayrollController.ts is a presentation file. Each method hands its work to business-layer services: PayrollService.submitHours, approve and run, and PayrollAuditService.log. Presentation may depend on business, so these calls are part of its role. The constructor parameters are business services injected into the controller, which counts as dependency wiring. HoursPayload is a request type the project declares itself, which fits presentation. The export method formats payslips through payslipRow, a presentation view, and joins the rows with '\n'. That is output formatting, not a calculation. The controller contains no domain invariant, calculation or decision: hours are not validated or computed, approval rules sit in the service, and payroll amounts are not worked out here. The controller does make the audit calls after submit and approve itself. I treat that as calling services, not owning a business rule, though it could be argued either way.
